body.p: This valuable study shows that mutants for the Notch ligand Jag2b lack brain pericytes, while heterozygous animals show reduced pericyte numbers and proliferation. It suggests Jag2b acts within a haemodynamic signalling pathway and Dll4 functionally opposes its proliferative role. The evidence is solid, however, further studies are required to resolve if the function represents direct endothelial-to-pericyte Notch signalling.
Summary:

Zi et al. investigate the role of Notch signaling during pericyte development in the brain. They show that mutants for Jag2b lack brain pericytes, while heterozygous animals show reduced pericyte numbers and proliferation. Expression of Jag2b relies on endothelial cell Notch activation, which is triggered through piezo-dependent hemodynamic signaling. Expression of the Notch ligand Dll4 in endothelial cells opposes Jag2b function and leads to a reduction in pericyte numbers.
Strengths:

Together, the data are of high quality with carefully controlled experiments and statistical analysis. They provide important new insights into the mechanisms regulating pericyte formation in the brain and will be of interest to a wide readership.
Weaknesses:
One complication is the effect of ligand manipulation on either endothelial cells or pericytes (or both).

(1) The authors show that new pericytes differentiate at the CVP region between 2 and 2.5 dpf, while Jag2b expression in CVP seems to be absent or very low in CVP endothelial cells during this time window. Can the authors speculate when and where pericyte progenitors encounter Jag2b-expressing cells necessary for their specification?

(2) The Jag2b heterozygous animals need to be better characterized. Is Jag2b expression reduced by 50% or is there compensation? Why is the initial specification process not affected in these mutants? If heterozygous animals would simply display hypomorphic mutant phenotypes, one would also expect a (small) phenotype during the initial specification step. Did the authors analyze initial specification in double Jag2b hets/dll4 homozygous mutants. Does Jag2b work independently of dll4 during the specification step?

(3) Lines 233-235. I do not think that the authors can conclude that Jag2b mainly regulates pericyte proliferation rather than ingression of pericytes into the brain. This is true for the heterozygous animals, in which proliferation is affected, but not ingression, but the homozygous animals show a very strong ingression/differentiation phenotype. To separate these two events, temporal control of Jag2b expression would provide valuable insights. It might also be informative to generate mosaic mutant embryos, where only some vessel segments are mutant for Jag2b and then follow ingression and proliferation of pericytes on these segments. If ingression is independent of Jag2b function, one would expect normal initial numbers of pericytes on those segments, but pericytes then fail to proliferate.
(4) Is endothelial cell Jag2b expression changed in dll4 homozygous mutants? Endothelial cell intrinsic Notch signalling should be lower in Dll4 mutants.
(5) Currently, the data lack direct evidence that either ligand binds to Notch receptors on pericytes.
Summary

Zi and colleagues investigate how endothelial Notch ligands regulate brain pericyte development. Combining single-cell transcriptomic reanalysis, genetic manipulations, pharmacological perturbations and live imaging, they identify Jag2b as a positive regulator of early pericerebral PDGFRB-positive cell emergence and subsequent brain pericyte expansion, whereas Dll4 exerts an opposing effect on proliferation. Genetic interaction and rescue experiments support a functional relationship in which Jag2b acts downstream of endothelial Notch and Piezo1. This is a substantial body of work, identifying a candidate endothelial mediator within the haemodynamics-Piezo1-Notch pathway. However, further evidence is required to determine whether Jag2b directly activates Notch in pericytes and whether the early specification phenotype is pericyte-specific rather than affecting a broader mural progenitor population. Clarification of the methodology and presentation of the underlying imaging data is also needed.
Strengths:

The authors present substantial data supporting Jag2b's function in endothelial-driven mural-cell development. Reciprocal loss- and gain-of-function experiments strengthen their hypotheses, and they effectively use previously published single-cell RNA sequencing datasets to identify candidate ligands. They generate several valuable transgenic lines to investigate endothelial-specific ligand expression and pathway manipulation and exploit the zebrafish model for live imaging. Genetic interaction experiments and pharmacological perturbations provide complementary evidence. The authors also acknowledge limitations concerning indirect vascular effects, mosaic transgene expression and conservation beyond zebrafish.
Weaknesses:

(1) The authors focus on the role of endothelial Notch signalling in brain pericyte development; however, they use a PDGFRB reporter that broadly labels mural cells, including vascular smooth muscle cells. Cells quantified around the BCA, PCS, and BA occupy basal arteries, and PDGFRB expression alone does not distinguish pericyte progenitors from immature mural cells that subsequently acquire vascular smooth muscle characteristics. Ando et al. (2019) established Notch-dependent mural cell specification in both cranial and trunk vessels, providing important context for these observations.

(2) The endothelial-to-pericyte signalling step requires further demonstration, as the authors do not show a direct readout of Notch activation in pericytes. Although the evidence provided is informative, it remains possible that the observed pericyte phenotypes arise from Jag2b acting within ECs and indirectly affecting pericytes without directly activating Notch in them.

(3) The authors performed a substantial amount of microscopy, which is in general appropriately displayed; however, there are many inconsistencies and a lack of detail in the figure legends, making a large and data-rich paper difficult to follow. Furthermore, in several instances where the authors state that time-lapse imaging was performed, the only output provided is a quantification graph without accompanying source movies or representative still images. Where imaging data for time-lapse experiments is provided, the quality of the movies is insufficient given the capabilities of modern zebrafish microscopy. These issues are particularly important for the key claims regarding brain pericyte proliferation and ingress.
Summary:

This manuscript aims to understand the role of Notch signaling, in particular via the Dll4 and Jag2b ligands, in pericyte differentiation and proliferation. The team uses zebrafish mutants coupled with transgenic tools to make their assessments.
Strengths:
Live imaging across stages of development using zebrafish is a strength.
Weaknesses:
(1) All images need to be made colorblind-accessible, and red changed to magenta.

(2) When generating the Jag2b transgenic line to assess cell-type-specific expression, the team does not rule out expression in pericytes. There is spotty expression in all of the images that needs to be confirmed as EC nuclei or similar, and not perivascular cells. This should be addressed. This should be fairly straightforward using their transgenic tools.

(3) Given that the jab2b knockout is global, the team should moderate their interpretation that the phenotype is solely driven by EC Jag2b unless they complete EC-specific rescue experiments to restore the pericyte specification defects. This is particularly important as the expression levels in the embryo during the time of pericyte specification are very low, and the team has already indicated that they believe the signal is permissive rather than instructive. The manuscript does state that this experiment was done; however, it is unclear what controls were used and how robust the response seen is for rescue back to WT control levels. The data, as it stands, is not very convincing.
(4) For the Jag2b+/- in Figure 3: there are fewer pericytes, but are they larger/have longer processes?

(5) The proliferation data is only assessed across a 12-hour window. This does not seem like a long enough window to accurately predict whether proliferation doesn't happen or if it's just a bit slower. This point should be addressed.
(6) In general, almost all experiments are missing a WT control condition as a comparator for rescue studies. Without this, it is hard to determine how meaningful the data is.
(7) Though the number of transgenic tools is impressive, the lack of consistent use of them between experiments limits drawing broader conclusions.
(8) The layout and inclusion of data in Figure 6 versus the supplement for this figure is confusing.

We sincerely thank the Reviewing Editor, Senior Editor, and three reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive evaluation of our manuscript. We appreciate their recognition of the value of our findings and the strengths of our genetic, imaging, and analytical approaches. We are particularly grateful for the suggestions that will help us further clarify the cellular specificity and mechanistic interpretation of endothelial Jag2b function during brain pericyte development.

disp-quote.p: (1) The authors show that new pericytes differentiate at the CVP region between 2 and 2.5 dpf, while Jag2b expression in CVP seems to be absent or very low in CVP endothelial cells during this time window. Can the authors speculate when and where pericyte progenitors encounter Jag2b-expressing cells necessary for their specification?

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. Pericyte differentiation in the CVP region begins at approximately 48 hpf. Initially, a subset of progenitor cells exhibits weak pdgfrb expression and is not in close contact with ECs. As these cells establish close contact with ECs, their pdgfrb expression increases markedly, and they gradually acquire characteristic pericyte morphology (Ando et al., 2016; Ando et al., 2019).

Given that canonical Notch signaling requires direct cell–cell contact between ligand-expressing and receptor-expressing cells, we speculate that Jag2b may begin to exert its function when these pdgfrb-low progenitor cells establish contact with ECs. This interaction may facilitate their differentiation into pericytes, accompanied by the upregulation of pdgfrb expression and the acquisition of specialized pericyte morphology. However, the precise timing and location of Jag2b-mediated signaling during this process remain to be determined.

disp-quote.p: (2) The Jag2b heterozygous animals need to be better characterized. Is Jag2b expression reduced by 50% or is there compensation? Why is the initial specification process not affected in these mutants? If heterozygous animals would simply display hypomorphic mutant phenotypes, one would also expect a (small) phenotype during the initial specification step. Did the authors analyze initial specification in double Jag2b hets/dll4 homozygous mutants. Does Jag2b work independently of dll4 during the specification step?

body.p: We thank the reviewer for these important questions. We are currently unable to quantitatively determine the extent to which jag2b expression is reduced in jag2b heterozygous mutants or whether compensatory mechanisms are involved.

Interestingly, we observed no significant changes in the initial pericyte specification process in jag2b heterozygous mutants, endothelial-specific jag2b-overexpressing larvae, dll4 knockout mutants, or endothelial-specific dll4-overexpressing larvae. In addition, jag2b reporter expression in the CVP region remains low at approximately 55 hpf, suggesting relatively weak reporter activity in this pericerebral progenitor niche during the specification period. Together, these observations are consistent with a stage-dependent role for Jag2b in pericyte development. Although Jag2b is required for efficient pericyte specification, increasing endothelial Jag2b expression does not appear sufficient to promote additional progenitor specification. This is consistent with a permissive rather than a strongly instructive role for Jag2b during the early specification stage.

We have not examined initial pericyte specification in jag2b heterozygous/dll4 homozygous double mutants. We agree that this analysis would be informative for determining whether Jag2b functions independently of Dll4 during the specification stage, and we consider this investigation for the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (3) Lines 233-235. I do not think that the authors can conclude that Jag2b mainly regulates pericyte proliferation rather than ingression of pericytes into the brain. This is true for the heterozygous animals, in which proliferation is affected, but not ingression, but the homozygous animals show a very strong ingression/differentiation phenotype. To separate these two events, temporal control of Jag2b expression would provide valuable insights. It might also be informative to generate mosaic mutant embryos, where only some vessel segments are mutant for Jag2b and then follow ingression and proliferation of pericytes on these segments. If ingression is independent of Jag2b function, one would expect normal initial numbers of pericytes on those segments, but pericytes then fail to proliferate.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful comment. We agree that our current data do not allow us to fully distinguish the effects of Jag2b on pericyte ingression and proliferation, particularly in jag2b homozygous mutants, which exhibit a severe defect in early pericyte specification.

We agree that temporally controlled manipulation of Jag2b expression or the generation of mosaic jag2b mutants, combined with longitudinal analysis of pericyte behavior, would provide valuable insights into the distinct roles of Jag2b in these processes. However, establishing these experimental systems and reliably identifying mutant vascular segments during live imaging present substantial technical challenges that are currently beyond the scope of this study.

We therefore acknowledge this limitation and have revised our interpretation to avoid concluding that Jag2b primarily regulates pericyte proliferation rather than ingression. Our findings support a role for Jag2b in early pericyte specification and indicate that Jag2b dosage also influences subsequent pericyte proliferation.

disp-quote.p: (4) Is endothelial cell Jag2b expression changed in dll4 homozygous mutants? Endothelial cell intrinsic Notch signalling should be lower in Dll4 mutants.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this important question. Unfortunately, the Ki((jag2b-EGFP) reporter line used in this study does not provide sufficient sensitivity and dynamic range to reliably detect potential changes in jag2b expression following dll4 loss-of-function. Furthermore, dll4 homozygous mutants do not survive to adulthood, making it challenging to obtain sufficient homozygous mutant larvae for the isolation of brain ECs and subsequent quantitative analysis of jag2b expression. Therefore, we are currently unable to determine whether endothelial jag2b expression is altered in dll4 homozygous mutants. We acknowledge that this remains an important question for understanding the regulatory relationship between Dll4 and Jag2b.

disp-quote.p: (5) Currently, the data lack direct evidence that either ligand binds to Notch receptors on pericytes.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for highlighting this important limitation. We agree that our current study does not provide direct evidence that Jag2b or Dll4 physically interacts with Notch receptors on pericytes. Previous studies using in vitro cell-based models have demonstrated interactions between endothelial JAG ligands and Notch3 receptors expressed by pericytes, providing a potential mechanistic basis for endothelial-to-pericyte Notch signaling (Liu et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2010). However, the limited availability of suitable antibodies for zebrafish makes it technically challenging to directly examine ligand–receptor interactions in vivo. We therefore acknowledge that our findings do not establish direct Jag2b- or Dll4-mediated activation of Notch receptors in pericytes. Rather, our data support the functional involvement of endothelial Notch ligands in regulating brain pericyte development, while the precise mechanisms underlying their effects remain to be elucidated.

disp-quote.p: (1) The authors focus on the role of endothelial Notch signalling in brain pericyte development; however, they use a PDGFRB reporter that broadly labels mural cells, including vascular smooth muscle cells. Cells quantified around the BCA, PCS, and BA occupy basal arteries, and PDGFRB expression alone does not distinguish pericyte progenitors from immature mural cells that subsequently acquire vascular smooth muscle characteristics. Ando et al. (2019) established Notch-dependent mural cell specification in both cranial and trunk vessels, providing important context for these observations.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We agree that PDGFRβ is not a pericyte-specific marker and is also expressed in vascular smooth muscle cells and other mural cell populations. Therefore, pdgfrb expression alone is insufficient to unequivocally distinguish pericyte progenitors from immature vascular smooth muscle cells, particularly during early developmental stages.

In our study, the identification of brain pericytes is based not only on pdgfrb expression but also on their anatomical location, cellular morphology, and dynamic behavior observed by live imaging. In particular, pericytes associated with brain microvessels exhibit characteristic elongated processes along the vascular surface, and their proliferation and expansion can be directly monitored during development.

Nevertheless, we acknowledge that the early pdgfrb-positive cells emerging around the CVP and basal cerebral arteries may represent a broader population of mural cell progenitors, whose eventual differentiation into pericytes or vascular smooth muscle cells cannot be definitively established from pdgfrb expression alone. We will revise the relevant descriptions to distinguish early mural cell emergence from subsequent brain pericyte development and expansion. We will clarify this limitation in the Discussion and taken into account previous studies demonstrating the involvement of Notch signaling in mural cell specification.

Importantly, these considerations do not alter our central finding that Jag2b regulates the development and expansion of brain pericytes, as supported by our genetic analyses and live imaging of pericytes associated with brain microvessels.

disp-quote.p: (2) The endothelial-to-pericyte signalling step requires further demonstration, as the authors do not show a direct readout of Notch activation in pericytes. Although the evidence provided is informative, it remains possible that the observed pericyte phenotypes arise from Jag2b acting within ECs and indirectly affecting pericytes without directly activating Notch in them.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that a direct readout of Notch activation in pericytes would be important for fully elucidating the signaling mechanism proposed in our study. However, the Notch reporter line currently available to us does not reliably detect an increase in Notch activity in brain pericytes following endothelial-specific jag2b overexpression. Therefore, establishing a more sensitive and suitable Notch reporter system would be necessary to directly assess Jag2b-dependent Notch activation in pericytes. We acknowledge this limitation and recognize that our current findings do not distinguish between direct activation of Notch signaling in pericytes and indirect effects mediated through endothelial cells. We have therefore revised the relevant interpretations to avoid presenting direct endothelial-to-pericyte Notch signaling as an established mechanism.

disp-quote.p: (3) The authors performed a substantial amount of microscopy, which is in general appropriately displayed; however, there are many inconsistencies and a lack of detail in the figure legends, making a large and data-rich paper difficult to follow. Furthermore, in several instances where the authors state that time-lapse imaging was performed, the only output provided is a quantification graph without accompanying source movies or representative still images. Where imaging data for time-lapse experiments is provided, the quality of the movies is insufficient given the capabilities of modern zebrafish microscopy. These issues are particularly important for the key claims regarding brain pericyte proliferation and ingress.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for these constructive comments. The time-lapse images included in our manuscript illustrate the processes of de novo pericyte specification and proliferation in the developing brain. These cellular behaviors have also been described in previous studies, and our purpose in presenting these examples was to illustrate the criteria used to identify pericyte division events.

In our experiments, we performed time-lapse imaging under different experimental conditions and quantified the frequency of pericyte division events. The primary objective of these analyses was to compare the occurrence of cell divisions across experimental groups, rather than to characterize differences in the morphological features of individual division events. Therefore, we believe that representative time-lapse sequences from each experimental condition would provide limited additional information beyond the quantitative analyses.

Regarding the video quality, because it was not possible to predict in advance which cells would undergo division or differentiate into pericytes during the subsequent 12-hour imaging period, we acquired time-lapse images covering the entire brain. The representative movies were subsequently generated by cropping specific regions of interest from these whole-brain datasets, which resulted in a reduction in the apparent spatial resolution of the exported videos. We acknowledge this technical limitation and appreciate the reviewer's concern regarding the clarity of the imaging data.

disp-quote.p: (1) All images need to be made colourblind-accessible, and red changed to magenta.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We will revise the color schemes throughout the manuscript to improve accessibility for readers with color vision deficiencies, including replacing red with magenta where appropriate.

disp-quote.p: (2) When generating the Jag2b transgenic line to assess cell-type-specific expression, the team does not rule out expression in pericytes. There is spotty expression in all of the images that needs to be confirmed as EC nuclei or similar, and not perivascular cells. This should be addressed. This should be fairly straightforward using their transgenic tools.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for raising this concern. In fact, we have carefully and repeatedly examined the fluorescence expression pattern of our endothelial-specific transgenic line. Across our imaging datasets, the H2B-mScarlet fluorescent reporter, which serves as a nuclear marker for endothelial cells, is predominantly localized to endothelial cell nuclei, and we have not observed H2B-mScarlet expression in pericytes. We will clarify this point in the revised manuscript to better explain the endothelial specificity of the transgenic reporter.

disp-quote.p: (3) Given that the jab2b knockout is global, the team should moderate their interpretation that the phenotype is solely driven by EC Jag2b unless they complete EC-specific rescue experiments to restore the pericyte specification defects. This is particularly important as the expression levels in the embryo during the time of pericyte specification are very low, and the team has already indicated that they believe the signal is permissive rather than instructive. The manuscript does state that this experiment was done; however, it is unclear what controls were used and how robust the response seen is for rescue back to WT control levels. The data, as it stands, is not very convincing.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this important comment. We agree that, because the jag2b knockout is global, the observed phenotype cannot be attributed exclusively to the loss of endothelial Jag2b without further evidence. To address the endothelial contribution of Jag2b, we performed endothelial-specific Jag2b rescue experiments in the jag2b mutant background. As shown in Figure 3—Figure Supplement 1F–G, endothelial-specific expression of Jag2b partially restored the number of brain pericytes in jag2b mutants. Although the rescue did not fully restore pericyte numbers to wild-type levels, these results support a functional contribution of endothelial-derived Jag2b to brain pericyte development.

We acknowledge that the incomplete rescue does not exclude potential contributions from Jag2b expressed in other cell types. In addition, differences in the timing, level, or spatial distribution of transgenic Jag2b expression may influence rescue efficiency. However, these possibilities remain to be experimentally determined.

We agree that direct comparison with wild-type controls is important for evaluating the extent of phenotypic rescue. We will therefore clarify the experimental controls and revise the presentation of the rescue data to facilitate comparisons between wild-type, mutant, and rescue conditions. We will also moderate our conclusions to avoid attributing the entire phenotype exclusively to endothelial Jag2b. Taken together, our findings support an important role for endothelial-derived Jag2b in brain pericyte development, while the potential contributions of Jag2b from other cellular sources remain to be investigated.

disp-quote.p: (4) For the Jag2b+/- in Figure 3: there are fewer pericytes, but are they larger/have longer processes?

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this interesting question. We did not observe an apparent increase in pericyte cell body size in jag2b heterozygous mutants. However, we noticed that the remaining pericytes tended to extend longer cellular processes. We speculate that this may be related to the reduced pericyte density, which could provide more space for individual pericytes to extend their processes along the vasculature.

disp-quote.p: (5) The proliferation data is only assessed across a 12-hour window. This does not seem like a long enough window to accurately predict whether proliferation doesn't happen or if it's just a bit slower. This point should be addressed.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this important comment. We agree that a 12-hour imaging window may not be sufficient to fully characterize pericyte proliferation dynamics, particularly when differences in proliferation rates between experimental groups are relatively subtle. Our 12-hour time-lapse imaging approach was primarily intended to detect differences in the frequency of pericyte division events between experimental conditions. This approach is more suitable for identifying substantial differences in proliferation over the observation period than for determining whether cell proliferation is completely abolished or merely delayed. We therefore acknowledge this limitation and will clarify that our conclusions are based on the frequency of cell division events observed within the 12-hour imaging window, rather than on the complete proliferative capacity of pericytes.

disp-quote.p: (6) In general, almost all experiments are missing a WT control condition as a comparator for rescue studies. Without this, it is hard to determine how meaningful the data is.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion. We agree that including wild-type controls is important for evaluating the extent and biological significance of phenotypic rescue. In fact, the corresponding wild-type control data for the experiments presented in Figures 5 and 6 were included in the supplementary figures. However, we recognize that their placement may have made it difficult for readers to directly compare the experimental groups. In the revised manuscript, we will reorganize the relevant figures and supplementary data to make these comparisons more straightforward. We will also include wild-type controls for additional rescue experiments wherever the corresponding data are available.

disp-quote.p: (7) Though the number of transgenic tools is impressive, the lack of consistent use of them between experiments limits drawing broader conclusions.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. We acknowledge that the use of different transgenic tools across experiments may limit direct comparisons and the generalizability of some conclusions. We agree that more consistent use of transgenic systems would further strengthen the interpretation of the results, and we will take this into consideration in future studies.

disp-quote.p: (8) The layout and inclusion of data in Figure 6 versus the supplement for this figure is confusing.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We agree that the current organization of Figure 6 and its supplementary figures could be improved. We will reorganize the relevant panels and supplementary data in the revised manuscript to improve the logical flow, clarity, and accessibility of the results.

We believe these revisions will strengthen the rigour and clarity of our study and help define more precisely how ligand-specific endothelial Notch signaling contributes to brain pericyte development. We thank the reviewers again for their constructive recommendations and look forward to submitting a carefully revised manuscript.
